statement: A logical ID is platform-independent and has exactly four levels. Provider names are derived from it; a name that changes when the platform changes is not a logical name. No provider-specific identifier (account id, cluster, region) appears in a human-facing name. A resource with no legal logical ID is the reason names drift; if a facet has no place in the hierarchy, the hierarchy gains a level rather than the facet gaining an invented name. A provider name carries identity only - what the resource is. Ownership, contact, purpose, lifecycle, provenance and consumers are attributes of that name, never parts of it, and they are recorded against the name in claims.entries. `system` is the top-level operational scope whose outcome the resource directly serves, and it is the only scope axis: `scope` is the derived `system` segment, never a second field that could contradict it. Its four terms are agency (autonomous agency operation and control), product (customer-facing products and datasets), tooling (development or operational tools that are not runtime substrate) and infrastructure (shared compute, networking, storage, identity and delivery substrate). Classification is by direct beneficiary, not implementation type: a product database is product, not infrastructure, and storage shared by several systems is infrastructure. Provenance is recorded in the vocabulary of W3C PROV - the record is the entity, a provisioning event is the activity, actor and actor_kind name the agent, and evidence attests the activity - so this registry carries no parallel provenance theory of its own.

level_terms.rule: A level term is defined here once, beside the level it belongs to, so no term is explained only in prose somewhere else. `system` is the top-level operational scope; a term appearing in two levels is a defect, because then one word means two things.

env.dev: A tier of a system that IS deployed per environment: the lowest tier, where work lands first.
env.stg: A tier of a system that IS deployed per environment: the middle tier, which exists to be rehearsed against before prod.
env.prod: A tier of a system that IS deployed per environment: the top tier, the one real users use.
env.shared: NOT deployed per environment; one instance serves every environment. `system` is what makes a resource a development environment, not `env`: the agency's dev, stg and prod work all share one developer environment, so there is exactly one of it and `env` only records that it is not tiered. `shared` is not a fourth tier and is never a synonym for prod.

level_terms.env_sibling_rule: `dev`, `stg` and `prod` are siblings of one another: naming one asserts the existence of the others, so a singleton that is stamped `dev` claims a `stg` and a bare-tier variant that will never exist. `shared` has no siblings, which is the point of the term.

namespaces.rule: platform and shared capability under alphaville-agency; product and dataset under alphaville-artifact; the frozen reference keeps alphaville-foundry as a recorded exception; a resource violating this is refused
namespaces.system_allows_rule: a namespace is chosen by the scope the resource serves, so a location must sit in a namespace whose system_allows list contains the record's system; alphaville-foundry is accepted for every system because it is frozen history rather than a live choice, and it is recorded here so it stops being copied by default

cloudflare_ai_gateway.note: the AI Gateway id shares the worker template deliberately: both are account-scoped resources in one flat namespace, so the same shape keeps them readable side by side. It is listed separately because the platform caps the id at 64 characters, not 63, and enforces its own character rules.

hostname.note: The bare label is owned by whichever env is NOT subordinate to another env of the same system; every env that has siblings above or beside it is prefixed, so two logical IDs cannot claim one hostname. `prod` takes the bare label because it is the top tier of a tiered system - a consequence of the rule, not an exception to it - and `shared` takes it because it is not tiered at all: prefixing a singleton would re-assert the existence of the `dev`/`stg`/`prod` siblings that `shared` exists to deny. `prefixed_envs` is the machine-readable half of this note, and the two are checked against each other by names/validate.py: every env term is either in `prefixed_envs` or owns the bare label.

hf_dataset.note: the repository type already carries dataset-vs-space; do not encode it in the name

cloudflare_container_app.note: A DECLARED name, and it took an explicit `name` in the Worker's containers[] entry to make it one. Left unset, the platform derives the application name as `<worker-name>-<lowercased class name>`, which is how this resource was called `dev-tooling-dsh-shell-sandbox`: the suffix came from the Sandbox SDK's class, not from us, so the name carried an SDK implementation detail and would have changed silently if that class were ever renamed. The template keeps the logical ID's `role` - it is the container application OF that role, not a role of its own - and appends `container` as the resource kind, because the registry's uniqueness rule is global across platforms and the Worker already renders the same base name. See declaredness.derived for what could not be owned.

declaredness.rule: A provider name is DECLARED when we choose it, so the serialisation is a decision this registry can be held to; it is DERIVED when a platform generates it from something this registry does not control, so the name is an observation rather than a decision. A derived name must be read back from the platform after provisioning and never inferred, because it can change without one character of this repository changing. A name a platform generates from someone else's class name is the sharpest case of that: nothing of ours appears in it at all.

derived.derivation: the Cloudflare managed registry names the image REPOSITORY after the container application, and the TAG after the Worker's deploy version, which is generated per deploy and has no logical ID to render from.
derived.consequence: the tag is not a name we own and not a name this registry can pin. The repository is ours only because the application name is ours, so it is derived-from-declared, and it is the reason `wrangler containers images list` has to be read rather than predicted.
derived.evidence: wrangler containers images list, run in the tooling repository on 2026-09-22

declaredness.history: Before `containers[].name` was set, the application AND its image repository were both derived as `<worker>-<lowercased class name>`, which is how this resource was called dev-tooling-dsh-shell-sandbox. The suffix came from the Sandbox SDK's class, not from us. That is recorded here rather than in a commit message because the derivation is a property of the platform, not of one deploy.
declaredness.enforced_by: names/validate.py --claims, which refuses a serialisation that is absent from `declared`

singletons.rule: An account-level resource that exists once per upstream identity does not render from a logical ID: env, system, component and role do not apply to it, because it is not ours to name. It is recorded here so its name is fixed by decision rather than drifting by default. Recording it is what keeps the four-level rule honest; the alternative is inventing levels for a resource that has no place in our hierarchy.

entries.name: cheapinference
entries.reason: AI Gateway custom-provider slug. It names the upstream provider, not an Alphaville resource, so it carries the provider's own identity and deliberately has no env prefix: one slug serves every gateway on the account.

entries.name: alphaville
entries.reason: The account's single Secrets Store. It is account-scoped and serves every environment, so it carries no env prefix and does not render from a logical id: it is the one place secrets live, which is the point of using it rather than scattering per-Worker secrets.

vocabularies.rule: Each closed vocabulary is defined here once and referenced by field name from the records and from the validator; a term list is never restated in a second place.
vocabularies.identity_rule: an identity consumer is identity:<identity>, and the identity vocabulary is the union of owner and contact, so no identity is defined twice
vocabularies.consumer_rule: a consumer is logical:<logical_id>, which must resolve to another record in this table, or identity:<identity>; an empty consumer list is forbidden, and a resource with no consumer must say so with no_consumers_reason, which is legal only when its code matches the lifecycle
vocabularies.source_rule: source_ref is registry:<logical_id> when this registry record is the only declaration of the resource, repo:<path> for a declaration in this repository, or github:<owner>/<repo>/<path> for a declaration elsewhere; nothing else resolves
vocabularies.no_exemption_rule: there is no foundational, internal, reserved-for-later or future-use exemption: a resource with no consumer is either planned or retired, or it is unused and refused

claims.rule: Every provider name this registry has been asked to reserve is recorded here with the logical ID that owns it and one authoritative resource record: who owns it, what it is for, where it lives, how it was provisioned and who consumes it. A name that is live on a platform but absent from this table is drift; the table is the record, not a decoration. occurred_at records the instant the provisioning act was recorded whenever the platform instant itself was not captured - each record's evidence file names that basis, so an approximate time is never presented as an observed one.

entries.purpose: Runs the cloud developer environment: the workspace an agent or the operator works in, which may disappear at any moment and which nothing in production may depend on. `system=tooling` is what makes it a development environment and `env=shared` records that it is not tiered - there is one, and it serves every environment. It replaced dev.tooling.dsh.shell, which is recorded as retired.
Runs the cloud developer environment: the workspace an agent or the operator works in, which may disappear at any moment and which nothing in production may depend on.

no_consumers_reason.detail: RETIRED 2026-09-22. Renamed to shared.tooling.dsh.shell: `dev` stamped a tier on a singleton and asserted a stg and a bare-tier sibling that do not and will not exist. The Worker, the container application, its images, the route and the R2 bucket were all deleted under these names before anything was rebuilt, so these names are reserved by nothing.

entries.purpose: The developer environment's model route, so model traffic from the workspace has one named gateway. Tooling is not tiered either, so this carries `shared` for the same reason its consumer does.
Routes the dev environment's model calls to the cheapinference custom provider, so model traffic from the developer workspace has one named route.

no_consumers_reason.detail: RETIRED 2026-09-22. Renamed to shared.tooling.dsh.gateway for the same reason as the Worker it served, and deleted as an orphan: its only intended consumer was the dev-named Worker, which no longer exists.

entries.purpose: The agency's own model route: the named AI Gateway the clean-slate build will call once it has a consumer.

no_consumers_reason.detail: Reserved for the clean-slate build: no runtime consumer calls this gateway yet, and no exemption is recorded for that, so it is planned until one does.

exceptions.reason: reference implementation, frozen; not renamed for aesthetics

uniqueness.rule: A provider name may be claimed by exactly one logical ID. Two logical IDs rendering onto the same provider name is refused, not resolved.
uniqueness.why: hostname, r2 and hf serialisations omit logical-ID levels by design, so uniqueness has to be enforced by reservation rather than assumed from the ID.
uniqueness.enforcement: the registry records claimed provider names; the validator rejects a second logical ID that renders onto an occupied name, naming both IDs and the name
